stem: A short magnetic dipole has magnetic moment 0.5 A m\(^{2}\). Calculate its magnetic field at a distance of 20 cm from the centre of magnetic dipole on (i) the axis (ii) the equatorial line (Given \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) SI units)
Earth's magnetic field at the equator is approximately \(4 \times 10^{-5}\) T. Calculate Earth's dipole moment. (Radius of Earth \(= 6.4 \times 10^{6}\) m, \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) SI units)
solution:
Given
\(B_{eq} = 4 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{T}\)
\(r = 6.4 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m}\)
Assume that Earth is a bar magnet with N and S poles being the geographical South and North poles, respectively. The equatorial magnetic field due to Earth's dipole can be written as
\(B_{eq} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}m}{4\pi r^{3}}\)
\(m = 4\pi B_{eq} \times r^{3} / \mu_{0}\)
\(= 4 \times 10^{-5} \times (6.4 \times 10^{6})^{3} \times 10^{7}\)
\(= 1.05 \times 10^{20}\,\text{A m}^{2}\)
_note: DEFECT (answer-affecting, transcribed VERBATIM per the brief): the final exponent is wrong. The book's own preceding line, 4e-5 x (6.4e6)^3 x 1e7, evaluates to 1.0486e23, not 1.05e20 — the mantissa 1.05 is right and only the exponent is a digit slip (20 for 23). 1.05e23 A m^2 is also the physically correct order for Earth's dipole moment (~8e22). Recorded in .solved-fixes.json + .errata.json.

stem:
At a given place on the Earth, a bar magnet of magnetic moment \(\vec{m}\) is kept horizontal in the East-West direction. P and Q are the two neutral points due to magnetic field of this magnet and \(\vec{B}_{H}\) is the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field.
(A) Calculate the angles between position vectors of P and Q with the direction of \(\vec{m}\).
(B) Points P and Q are 1 m from the centre of the bar magnet and \(B_{H} = 3.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{T}\). Calculate the magnetic dipole moment of the bar magnet.
Neutral point is that point where the resultant magnetic field is zero.
solution:
(A) As seen from the figure, the direction of magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) due to the bar magnet is opposite to \(\vec{B}_{H}\) at the points P and Q. Also, \((\theta + \alpha) = 90^{0}\) at P and it is \(270^{0}\) at Q.
\(\tan\alpha = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan\theta\)
\(\therefore \tan\theta = 2\tan\alpha\)
\(= 2\tan(90 - \theta)\) and \(2\tan(270 - \theta)\)
\(\therefore \tan\theta = \pm 2\cot\theta\)
\(\therefore \tan^{2}\theta = 2\)
\(\therefore \tan\theta = \pm\sqrt{2}\)
\(\therefore \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\pm\sqrt{2}\right)\)
\(\therefore \theta = 54^{0}44'\) and \(180^{0} - 54^{0}44^{0} = 116^{0}4\)

(B)
\(\tan^{2}\theta = 2\)
\(\therefore \sec^{2}\theta = 1 + \tan^{2}\theta = 1 + 2 = 3\)
\(\therefore \cos^{2}\theta = \dfrac{1}{3}\)
\(r = 1\,\text{m}\) and \(B = B_{\text{H}} = 3.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{T}\) (Given)
we have,
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{r^{3}}\sqrt{3\cos^{2}\theta + 1}\)
\(\therefore m = \dfrac{B_{\text{H}} \times r^{3}}{\left(\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\right)\sqrt{3\cos^{2}\theta + 1}}\)
\(= \dfrac{3.5 \times 10^{-5} \times 1^{3}}{10^{-7} \times \sqrt{3\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + 1}}\)
\(\therefore m = \dfrac{350}{\sqrt{2}} = 247.5\,\text{A m}^{2}\)
_note: DEFECT (answer-affecting, transcribed VERBATIM): part (A)'s closing line prints 180 deg - 54 deg 44' = 116 deg 4. The correct supplement is 125 deg 16' (180 - 54.7356 = 125.2644 deg = 125 deg 16'). The same line also prints a degree sign where a prime belongs (54 deg 44 deg). Part (B) is arithmetically CORRECT (350/sqrt2 = 247.487 = 247.5). Recorded in .solved-fixes.json + .errata.json. The printed solution also opens 'As seen from the figure' and carries an embedded neutral-point diagram on p-06 which is NOT attached — flagged as a solution-image candidate.
